text: Typing a five-row DataFrame by hand was fine for learning. Real work starts with a file — a CSV export from a system, a download from a colleague, a dump from a database. This lesson covers how to load a CSV into pandas, and just as important, the short inspection routine you should run on every dataset before you trust it.

Load a file with pd dot read underscore csv, passing the path — orders dot c-s-v here. This small orders table has eight rows: an order id, a customer id, a date, an amount, and a status. Notice order 5 has an empty amount, on purpose — real data is never perfectly complete, and that's exactly the kind of thing this inspection routine catches.

Step one: look at the edges. Orders dot head of 3 shows the first three rows — order id, customer id, date, amount, status, all lining up as expected. Head and tail default to 5 rows if you don't pass a number. Checking both the head and the tail catches files where the header got mangled, or where someone appended a total row at the very bottom.

Step two: orders dot info parentheses for structure. It reports eight entries total, but the amount column shows only 7 non-null — one value is missing, exactly the empty cell we planted. And order underscore date shows up as dtype object, meaning pandas read the dates as plain text rather than real dates. That's the single most common surprise in freshly loaded data.

Step three: orders dot describe for numbers. For each numeric column you get the count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles, and maximum — amount shows a count of 7, a minimum of 45, a maximum of 310. Scan for values that make no business sense, like a negative amount. Notice describe also happily summarizes order underscore id and customer underscore id, even though averaging an ID means nothing — pandas can't know which numbers are really labels, so that judgment is yours. Pass include equals object to summarize text columns instead.

Step four: orders dot isna parentheses dot sum. Isna returns a table of True-False flags for every cell, and sum adds up the Trues per column — here, zero missing everywhere except amount, which has exactly one. This is the quickest way to see how much is missing and precisely where.

Often you can fix issues right at load time instead of afterward. Pass parse underscore dates with a list of column names to convert them to real dates, usecols to keep only the columns you actually need, and nrows to read just the first few rows of a huge file so you can explore quickly. Reload with parse underscore dates on order underscore date, and dot-dtypes now shows datetime64 instead of object — we'll use it properly in the dates lesson.

To recap: load with read underscore csv, then always run the routine — head and tail for the edges, info for types and non-null counts, describe for numeric ranges, and isna dot sum for missing values. Two minutes of inspection tells you exactly what cleaning lies ahead. Next, we learn to select exactly the rows and columns we want.
